ansible-basics-inventory-and-ad-hoc.r: An engineer needed to check the disk space on forty servers during an incident. One ad-hoc command against the inventory group returned all forty answers in seconds, with no agent installed anywhere.
ansible-basics-inventory-and-ad-hoc.x: Agentless is convenient and shifts load to the control host, SSH and its credentials. Keep inventory as the source of truth, limit who can run ad-hoc commands and prefer playbooks for anything you would repeat.

playbooks-tasks-and-idempotence.r: A playbook that appended a line to a config file on every run made the file grow each time. Using a module that ensures the line exists made repeated runs change nothing the second time.
playbooks-tasks-and-idempotence.x: Idempotence is the test of good automation. Prefer modules over shell commands, use check mode and diff, and make changed status meaningful so reports tell the truth.

variables-facts-and-templates.r: A template used a variable with the wrong precedence and an old default overrode the intended value on production only. Listing where each variable is defined, and keeping fewer layers, made values predictable.
variables-facts-and-templates.x: Variable precedence is a major source of surprise. Keep a small number of places for values, name variables with a role prefix, validate required inputs and avoid logic-heavy templates.

handlers-conditionals-and-loops.r: A service was restarted after every run even when nothing changed, causing brief blips. Moving the restart into a handler notified only on a real change removed the blips.
handlers-conditionals-and-loops.x: Handlers run late and once, which helps and surprises. Know when they flush, use conditions on facts you trust and be careful with loops that hide partial failure.

roles-and-collections.r: Ten teams each wrote their own web server setup and fixes never spread. A shared role, versioned and tested, let a security fix reach every team through an update.
roles-and-collections.x: Roles are APIs: keep them focused, document inputs, pin versions and test them in isolation. Avoid deep dependency chains and decide who owns each shared role.

vault-secrets-and-safe-practice.r: A vault password was written in a shared document so people could run playbooks. When the document leaked, every secret had to be rotated. A secrets manager with per-person access would have avoided it.
vault-secrets-and-safe-practice.x: Vault protects files at rest but you still own the password. Limit access, use different vaults per environment, keep secrets out of logs with no_log and rotate when people leave.

ansible-at-scale.r: A change was run on all two hundred servers at once and a bad setting took them all down. Running in small serial batches with a health check between them would have stopped it at the first failure.
ansible-at-scale.x: At scale, concurrency is a risk. Use serial batches, canary hosts, max failure limits and health checks, tune forks and connection reuse, and decide how Ansible and Terraform divide the work.

dynamic-inventory-for-cloud.r: A static inventory listed servers that had been replaced weeks earlier, so a run skipped the new ones. A dynamic inventory built from cloud tags always matched what actually existed.
dynamic-inventory-for-cloud.x: Inventory from the source of truth avoids drift, but your tagging becomes critical. Standardise tags, cache carefully and test what happens when the cloud API is slow or returns partial data.

testing-and-linting-ansible.r: A small typo in a variable name passed review and failed in production at the worst moment. Running ansible-lint and a test in a throwaway container on every pull request caught the next one in seconds.
testing-and-linting-ansible.x: Test roles on the platforms you support, check idempotence by running twice and keep tests quick. A test that is slow or flaky will be skipped.

debugging-ansible-runs.r: A playbook failed on one host with an unreachable error. Running with more verbosity showed the host's SSH key had changed after a rebuild. Updating the known hosts entry fixed it in a minute.
debugging-ansible-runs.x: Raise verbosity gradually, run against one host, use the debugger and check facts and variable values before blaming the module. Record the cause so the next person finds it faster.
